14:                                                    Abstract. Consider a society of voters, each of whom specify an approval
15:                                                    set over a linear political spectrum. We examine double-interval societies, in
16:                                                    which each person’s approval set is represented by two disjoint closed intervals,
17:                                                    and study this situation where the approval sets are pairwise-intersecting:
18:                                                    every pair of voters has a point in the intersection of their approval sets. The
19:                                                    approval ratio for a society is, loosely speaking, the popularity of the most
20:                                                    popular position on the spectrum. We study the question: what is the minimal
21:                                                    guaranteed approval ratio for such a society? We provide a lower bound for the
22:                                                    approval ratio, and examine a family of societies that have rather low approval
23:                                                    ratios. These societies arise from double-n strings: arrangements of n symbols
24:                                                    in which each symbol appears exactly twice.

29:                                                                                 1. Introduction
30:                                                Consider the voting model of Berg et. al.[1] in which a political spectrum X is
31:                                           viewed as a continuum, with liberal positions on the left and conservative positions
32:                                           on the right, and in which each voter v “approves” an interval of positions along
33:                                           this line. For example, a tolerant moderate might approve a wide interval near the
34:                                           middle of the line, while an intolerant partisan may approve a narrower interval
35:                                           near one of the ends.
36:                                                More formally, a society is a spectrum X together with a set of voters V and
37:                                           a collection of approval sets {Av }, one for each voter. A point on the spectrum X
38:                                           is called a platform. In our situation, we imagine X to be R, and each approval set
39:                                           Av is a closed interval that represents the set of all platforms that v approves.
40:                                                Now suppose that every pair of people can agree on some platform; that is, their
41:                                           intervals overlap. In this situation, Helly’s Theorem [3] implies that there exists a
42:                                           point on the line that lies in everyone’s approval set, i.e., there is a platform that
43:                                           everyone approves. Thus a strong hypothesis (pairwise intersecting sets) produces
44:                                           a strong conclusion (a point in all the sets). However, in voting theory, we are
45:                                           usually not looking for unanimity, but may be satisfied with a platform that has
46:                                           high approval ratio: the fraction of voters that approve this platform.
47:                                                Various authors have relaxed the hypotheses. Berg et. al.[1] define a linear
48:                                           (k, m)-agreeable society in which voter preferences again are modeled by closed

76:     We generalize the one-interval model to a society in which every member is
77: identified with two disjoint approval intervals and call such a society a double-
78: interval society. This situation may arise naturally in the context of voting to
79: account for voters who do not place candidates along a linear spectrum in exactly
80: the same order, or to account for voters who find disjoint sets of platforms appealing
81: for entirely different reasons (e.g., for being a party purist, or having the ability
82: to work across party lines). In a scheduling context, such intervals might model a
83: society of workers, each of whom has two different work shifts.
84:     Figure 1 illustrates a double-interval society with four voters. The approval
85: sets of each voter have been separated vertically so they are easier to see. Note
86: that the approval sets are pairwise-intersecting: each voter overlaps every other
87: voter in one or both of their approval intervals. In this example, there are several
88: platforms approved by three voters, but no platform is approved by all four. The
89: approval number of a platform a(p) is the number of voters (in a society S) who
90: approve of platform p. The approval number of a society a(S) is the maximum
91: approval number over all platforms in the spectrum X. That is
92:                                   a(S) = max a(p).

95: Finally, define the approval ratio of a society to be the approval number of S divided
96: by the number of voters in S.
97:      The main question we address in this paper is: what is the minimal approval
98: ratio of a pairwise-intersecting, double-interval society with n voters?
99:      Examples suggest that the minimal approval ratio of such societies is 1/3; that
100: is, there is always a platform that will get at least a third of the votes. Our results
101: in this paper attempt to clarify this intuition.
